before.tldr: An inactive look-alike treatment given to the comparison group in a trial so that neither patients nor doctors can tell who is on the real drug. In cancer trials it is added on top of standard treatment, never given instead of it.
before.summary: Placebos control for the placebo effect (improvement from expectation), for the extra attention trial patients receive, and for bias in how symptoms and side effects are reported; in oncology a placebo arm nearly always means 'standard of care plus placebo' versus 'standard of care plus new drug', since withholding effective treatment would be unethical. Placebo-controlled designs are most common in adjuvant and maintenance settings where the comparator is observation, and they are impossible when the new drug's side effects give it away. When an active standard exists, trials compare against it directly (open-label or double-dummy) rather than using placebo.

after.tldr: A placebo is an inactive comparison treatment. A cancer trial may compare standard care plus placebo with standard care plus a new drug, or use another justified design. The protocol and consent explain what each group receives.
after.summary:
A placebo is an inert substance without pharmacological activity. In a blinded randomised trial, keeping participants and investigators unaware of assignment can reduce biased observations, especially for subjective outcomes. It does not guarantee that treatment remains concealed: characteristic adverse effects can reveal or suggest the assignment.

FDA's August 2019 cancer-trial guidance describes selected uses, including add-on designs and settings where surveillance is standard care or no treatment is available. Replacing an available effective therapy with placebo alone is a different ethical question from adding placebo to standard care. NCI explains that a study can compare standard treatment plus placebo with standard treatment plus the study drug. Read the actual groups, protocol and consent rather than inferring no care, a guaranteed active drug or a universal trial design.

The FDA guidance recommends planned unblinding in specified circumstances, including documented progression when appropriate treatment alternatives exist and suspected drug-related adverse events whose management would involve substantial toxicity or invasive procedures. These are guidance recommendations with stated qualifications, not a rule that every trial must remain blinded or that visible side effects make blinding categorically impossible.

notes: For research planning, distinguish a hard dependency from a scheduling preference. A hard dependency is an input, permission or required check without which the named step cannot proceed under its stated rules; a preference is an order the team would like. Reversibility is a different question. A mandatory analysis can be revisable, while an optional experiment can consume irreplaceable tissue. Copies of a DNA or RNA dataset can inform different target searches, but copying data does not replace the physical specimen, permission to use it or separate product validation.

In a fictional worksheet, Lab A accepts existing DNA and RNA data, their quality report and permitted reuse for candidate ranking. It needs neither new tissue nor Lab B's result. Lab B has confirmed that the preparation and selected region of an archived formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded block fit its protein-localisation study; it requires four sections. The custodian has identified six research sections after protecting diagnostic needs, but release is unconfirmed. A joint meeting after both reports is a scheduling preference, not an input either lab requires.

Under those invented constraints, Lab A can start while the team asks the custodian about Lab B's release. The inquiry uses no tissue. Cutting and consuming four sections requires release and the agreed specimen requirements to remain satisfied; consumed material is not restored by returning the block. Six minus four leaves two sections in this exercise, without predicting assay yield, successful analysis or future adequacy. A fixed block does not establish a viable-cell input. Preserve original data, record use and keep permission, input acceptance and an informative result separate.

Candidate-ranking data do not establish an accessible surface protein or a clinically useful product. Surface-target research still needs localisation, accessibility and normal-tissue assessment; T-cell receptor sequences still need functional specificity testing. A target-specific experiment needs a defined question and target. A product-specific potency or safety test needs the actual candidate being tested, and batch release needs a defined manufacturing process and its quality requirements. Process development and documentation can overlap, so a planning diagram supplies no universal order for all safety and manufacturing work. No product, combination comparison or clinical administration plan is supplied by the fictional two-laboratory worksheet.

notes: Reading a combination result. A combination rationale should name the job of each component (for example a growth pathway, a survival route, a location or stage, or a resistant population), and each story makes predictions that need testing. A regimen that beats one component does not show which component supplied the benefit, nor superiority to every alternative. In ASCENT-04 (443 people with previously untreated locally advanced or metastatic triple-negative breast cancer whose tumours express PD-L1, combined positive score 10 or higher), median progression-free survival was 11.2 months with sacituzumab govitecan plus pembrolizumab and 7.8 months with physician's-choice chemotherapy plus pembrolizumab (hazard ratio 0.65, 95 per cent CI 0.51 to 0.84; label section 14); that compares the ADC with chemotherapy as pembrolizumab's partner and does not by itself show synergy. Independent drug action offers another explanation: if each person benefits from the drug to which their tumour is most sensitive, patient-to-patient variability alone can explain the superiority of many approved combinations without additivity or synergy (Palmer and Sorger), which is an alternative explanation, not a rule that effective combinations lack synergy. A combination can also add toxicity, change exposure or force lower doses, and simultaneous and sequential treatment are different strategies that a molecular diagram cannot choose between.

What 'synergy' means and how it is measured. Synergy is the narrower claim that a combined effect exceeds a stated reference expectation, and the references differ. Highest single agent (Gaddum) expects the better single effect and is the easiest bar to clear. Bliss independence expects the probability of being unaffected by each drug to be independent, so for effects written as fractions the expectation is A plus B minus A times B. Loewe additivity treats the two drugs as dilutions of one another and needs the full dose-response curve of each, with straight-line isoboles as its classic form. In Chou's median-effect method a combination index below 1 indicates synergism, equal to 1 additivity and above 1 antagonism, within that method only. Meyer et al. found no consensus on how to quantify synergy, and Yadav et al. note that a drug combined with itself can easily exceed the highest single agent and that their zero-interaction potency score is zero when both independence and dose additivity hold. A 2020 review's point stands: a synergy claim needs its model, scale and uncertainty named. Greco's 1995 review was identified but only its title could be read. Laboratory interaction analysis needs single-drug dose-response data, combination conditions, controls and variation estimates; a clinical survival advantage does not by itself measure a cell-level interaction.

The two fictional comparisons use different units of inference. In a ten-tumour better-component model, A covers tumours 1 to 4 and B covers 3 to 6: 4 + 4 - 2 = 6 in the union, with four in neither group. There is no extra within-tumour interaction or added toxicity in that counting model. Separately, one cultured-cell experiment at 72 hours gives 20%, 30% and 40% inhibition for A, B and the pair at one fixed dose pair. Inhibition here is a reduction in vehicle-normalised viable-cell count, not a direct death measurement. HSA expects 30% and Bliss 44%, so 40% exceeds the first and falls below the second. Loewe needs single-drug dose-response curves; three numbers and no uncertainty estimate cannot establish a general synergy claim. In this model, greater overlap among responders reduces the union. Independent drug action does not require the two response groups to be statistically independent; shared resistance and response correlation matter to a population prediction.
